title: Maximal correlation of Lévy bridges
shortTitle: Pinning a random path’s endpoint can create dependence
oneLine: For a two-dimensional Lévy process pinned at its endpoint, the maximal correlation of the coordinate paths is the largest of three numbers, and jump times matter only through shared jumps; an operator-form answer to a question of Chang and Chen.
abstract: The maximal correlation of two random objects is the largest correlation between any function of the first and any function of the second. Chang and Chen (The Annals of Applied Probability, 2026) computed it for the two coordinate paths of a two-dimensional Lévy process and asked, in their Section 6, Problem 1, for the answer when the process is pinned at a terminal point, that is, for a Lévy bridge. This candidate shows that the bridge coefficient is the largest of three numbers: the absolute correlation of the Gaussian part; the maximal correlation of the two unordered lists of jump sizes; and the norm of an operator that counts common jumps. Jump times therefore matter only through which jumps are shared. A one-cut principle follows: once the jump sizes are retained, knowing which jumps occur before one fixed time preserves the coefficient, and two different cut times shrink the common-jump and Gaussian terms by an explicit factor. The formula holds for almost every endpoint, for every endpoint when the Gaussian covariance is positive definite (standard bridge) and at every atom of the endpoint law; infinite jump activity is allowed. The two jump terms are operator norms with no general elementary formula; they are made concrete without common jumps (a two-dimensional problem for the jump totals; pure-jump coordinates become independent), for finitely many lattice jump vectors (finite matrices) and for Chang and Chen's pinned compound-Poisson Examples 2-4 (coefficient one wherever the second coordinate jumps). Without pinning the same machinery reproves Chang and Chen's formula on every finite horizon. The engine is a correlation identity for marks attached to the classes of a hidden random matching, of which Chang and Chen's Theorem 1.5 is essentially the visible-matching case. Pinning can raise the coefficient from 0.2 to above 0.997 without common jumps, and can also lower it. Limits: a reduction, not a closed formula; no claim at exceptional endpoints; every-endpoint statements for gamma or stable bridges remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 2.1 (proof, main): for terminal-law almost every z, R_z(X, Y) = max{ρ_G, c_0(z), c_1(z)}: the Gaussian correlation, the maximal correlation of the jump-size lists, and the norm of the common-jump operator; also at every z for positive-definite Gaussian covariance (standard bridge) and at every atom. This answers Chang and Chen’s Section 6, Problem 1 in operator form.

Corollary 2.2 (proof, main): one-cut principle; the jump sizes, their before/after split at one fixed time s and the Gaussian bridge values at s give the full coefficient for every s; two different cut times multiply the common-jump and Gaussian terms by the Brownian-bridge correlation θ(s, t).

Theorem 3.1 (proof, main): for marks attached to the classes of a hidden random partial matching, R = max{R(static data), ‖K‖}; Chang and Chen’s Theorem 1.5 is essentially the visible-matching special case; a hidden swap has R = 1/√2 against 1 when revealed.

Propositions 5.1-5.3 and Corollary 5.4 (proof): finite matrices for finitely many lattice jump vectors; without common jumps c_0 is the maximal correlation of the jump totals and pure-jump coordinates are independent; unconditioned c_1 = Op(ν), c_0 ≤ Op(ν), reproving Chang and Chen’s formula; their pinned Examples 2-4 have coefficient 1 wherever Y jumps.

Examples (Section 6): a four-type bridge where the dominant jump term switches at c = 1/4; a shared-shock Poisson bridge where pinning lowers the coefficient; a Gaussian-Poisson bridge where pinning raises it from 0.2 to a value certified in (0.997457967473837283247, 0.997457967473837283251).

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about how much two random paths can tell us about each other when they are forced to finish at a chosen point.

Maximal correlation measures how much one random quantity can reveal about another, using any functions of them, not just straight-line relationships. A value of zero means the two are independent, and a value of one means they share something exactly.

Chang and Chen worked out this coefficient for the two coordinates of a Lévy process, which is random motion made of continuous wiggles plus sudden jumps. They then asked what happens for a Lévy bridge, where the same motion is pinned to end at a given point. Pinning changes the picture: it destroys independence over time and can create dependence where there was none. In one example, the two sides jump independently and their wiggles are only weakly correlated, so the coefficient is point two; once both ends are pinned, it rises above point nine nine seven, close to perfect dependence.

The answer in this paper is that the bridge coefficient is the largest of three numbers: the correlation of the wiggles, how dependent the two lists of jump sizes are, and a measure of how often the two coordinates jump at the same moment. Exact timing matters only through those shared jumps. A one-cut principle follows: keep the jump sizes, note which jumps happen before one fixed time, and nothing is lost.

The key idea is that, once the jump sizes are known, the jump times behave like independent uniform clocks, except that a shared jump shares its clock; and statistics that use several shared clocks never beat those that use a single clock.

There are clear limits. The size term and the shared-jump term are operator norms, with no general formula. They become concrete when the coordinates never jump together, or when there are finitely many whole-number jump types. Statements at every endpoint for gamma or stable bridges remain open, and pinning can raise the coefficient or lower it.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and computer calculations rather than by peer review, and this briefing uses a synthetic voice that is not additional evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Chang and Chen (2026), On the maximal correlation of some stochastic processes. The Annals of Applied Probability. The formula for unconditioned Lévy processes (Theorem 1.2), reproved here on every finite horizon; the labelled random-subset theorem (Theorem 1.5), essentially the visible-matching case of the identity here; and the question for Lévy bridges (Section 6, Problem 1), answered here in operator form.

Diaconis and Griffiths (2012), Exchangeable pairs of Bernoulli random variables, Krawtchouck polynomials, and Ehrenfest urns. Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics. The fixed-overlap Krawtchouk spectrum and the random-elements-in-common construction behind the shared-shock example.
Griffiths and Milne (1978), A class of bivariate Poisson processes. Journal of Multivariate Analysis. The class of bivariate Poisson processes to which the unpinned shared-shock pair belongs.

Griffiths, Milne and Wood (1979), Aspects of correlation in bivariate Poisson distributions and processes. Australian Journal of Statistics. Ranges of ordinary correlation for bivariate Poisson laws and processes.

Madiman and Barron (2007), Generalized Entropy Power Inequalities and Monotonicity Properties of Information. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. The analysis-of-variance decomposition for random subsets used in Section 3.

Guo and Zhang (2022), Extreme eigenvalues of nonlinear correlation matrices with applications to additive models. Stochastic Processes and their Applications. Binomial overlap coefficients for symmetric functions of overlapping samples (Theorem 3).

Kallenberg (1973), Canonical representations and convergence criteria for processes with interchangeable increments. Zeitschrift für Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und Verwandte Gebiete. The canonical representation behind the uniform-clock description of jumps.
Chaumont and Uribe Bravo (2015), Shifting Processes with Cyclically Exchangeable Increments at Random. Progress in Probability. The restatement of Kallenberg’s representation used in Section 4.
Last and Penrose (2017), Lectures on the Poisson Process. Cambridge University Press. Poisson marking, the Mecke equation and the Fock-space representation.
